package_info.why_malicious: MikuBot is a Windows-based malware bot that performs credential theft, enables unauthorized remote access, propagates via USB drives, and downloads or executes additional malicious payloads. It uses anti-detection techniques such as encrypted resource sections, dynamic API resolution, and anti-emulation, and is distributed as a commercial crimeware toolkit.

execution_context.file_location: RCData section of the Windows PE resource section

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (on initial execution), the code locates the encrypted payload in the RCData resource section, decrypts it in memory, and loads the UPX-packed payload for execution, resulting in the unpacked malware running in the process context.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Storing encrypted executable payloads in the resource section and decrypting them at runtime is a technique commonly used by malware to evade static analysis and detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not typically self-decrypt and execute hidden payloads from resource sections, as this behavior is associated with code obfuscation and malicious intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some DRM-protected or anti-tamper software may use similar resource encryption and runtime decryption for intellectual property protection, but not for self-executing hidden payloads.
key_indicators: Encrypted payload embedded in RCData section

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after payload unpacking), the code creates a uniquely named mutex in process memory to ensure only one instance of the malware runs, terminating the process if the mutex already exists, thereby preventing multiple infections and maintaining code integrity.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware frequently uses mutexes with unique or random names to prevent reinfection and to coordinate persistence mechanisms.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: While legitimate applications may use mutexes for single-instance enforcement, they do not typically use randomly generated or malware-specific names tied to persistence.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may use mutexes to enforce single-instance operation, but with predictable or application-specific names and not for persistence coordination.
key_indicators: Immediate process termination if mutex exists

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode: Create scheduled task for persistence
schtasks /Create /SC MINUTE /MO 10 /TN "MikuBotMutexName" /TR "C:\Path\To\MikuBot.exe"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (persistence setup), the code creates a scheduled task in the Windows Task Scheduler named after the mutex, configured to execute the malware every 10 minutes, ensuring the malware persists and re-executes even after system reboots.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Creating scheduled tasks for frequent self-execution is a well-known malware persistence technique, especially when the task name is tied to a mutex or is otherwise non-descriptive.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely schedules itself to run at high frequency (e.g., every 10 minutes) without explicit user consent or clear operational need.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System maintenance or update tools may use scheduled tasks, but typically with clear user intent, descriptive names, and less frequent intervals.
key_indicators: Scheduled task creation with malware-specific or random name

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (during data exfiltration), the code collects sensitive information from the victim's system, such as credentials or files, and transmits the data via HTTP POST to a remote command and control server, resulting in unauthorized data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating sensitive data to an external, attacker-controlled server is a primary indicator of information-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not collect and transmit user data to unknown or untrusted remote servers without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Crash reporting or telemetry tools may send limited diagnostic data, but only with user consent and to trusted domains.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP POST requests to untrusted or hardcoded domains

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode: Launch hidden VNC session
StartHiddenVNCSession(); // Accepts remote connections for control
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (during remote access), the code launches a hidden VNC server session in process memory, enabling remote actors to connect and control the victim's machine without user notification, resulting in unauthorized remote access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Launching a hidden VNC server for remote control is a core capability of remote access trojans (RATs) and is highly indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate remote access tools require user consent, provide visible notifications, and use secure authentication.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT support or remote administration tools may use VNC, but always with user awareness and explicit permission.
key_indicators: No user notification or consent for remote access

execution_context.file_location: main process memory, USB device mount points

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (during propagation), the code enumerates all connected USB drives, copies its executable to each drive as 'MikuBot.exe', and sets up autorun configuration, resulting in the malware spreading to new hosts via removable media.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-propagation via USB drives and autorun setup is a classic worm technique used to spread malware across systems.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not silently copy itself to removable drives or create autorun entries without user intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Portable applications may be copied to USB drives by users, but do not self-replicate or set up autorun without explicit action.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (when instructed by the attacker), the code retrieves a URL for a new payload, downloads the file from the Internet to a temporary directory, and executes it, resulting in further system compromise with additional malware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing arbitrary code from the Internet is a primary method for malware to escalate privileges, install additional payloads, or update itself.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software updaters only download signed, trusted payloads and require user consent before execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may download and execute updates, but with digital signature verification and user approval.
key_indicators: Arbitrary file download from remote URL
Silent execution of newly downloaded binaries

attack_chain.action: Malware is executed, decrypts and loads its payload from the resource section.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload is unpacked and executed in memory.

attack_chain.action: Creates a mutex to ensure only one instance runs and to protect code integrity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Prevents multiple infections and coordinates persistence.

attack_chain.action: Establishes persistence by creating a scheduled task to run every 10 minutes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ensures malware re-executes even after reboot.

attack_chain.leads_to: Infection spreads to new hosts via removable media.

attack_chain.leads_to: System may be further compromised with new payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Executable decrypts and loads payload from RCData resource section at runtime
Creation of uniquely named mutexes to prevent multiple instances
Scheduled task creation for frequent self-execution (every 10 minutes) with non-descriptive or random names
Hidden VNC server launched without user notification or consent
Enumeration and writing of self-copy to USB drives as 'MikuBot.exe' with autorun setup
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded or suspicious C2 domains
Download and silent execution of additional binaries from the Internet
file_indicators: Presence of encrypted data in RCData section of PE files
Scheduled tasks with unusual or random names matching mutex
Unexpected autorun.inf files on removable media
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled C2 domains (e.g., http://malicious-c2.com/upload)
Unusual VNC traffic originating from infected hosts on non-standard ports
Frequent outbound connections to untrusted domains immediately after process startup
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for executables that decrypt and execute payloads from their RCData resource sections, create mutexes with random or suspicious names, and establish scheduled tasks for frequent self-execution. Detect hidden VNC server activity and USB propagation behaviors by monitoring for self-copies and autorun files on removable media. Use network monitoring to identify outbound HTTP POST requests to untrusted domains and VNC traffic from non-standard ports. Correlate these behaviors to identify and respond to MikuBot infections.
